      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>? <p><span class="qt0">Head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> is the name for <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> that develop in the mouth, nose and sinuses, salivary glands, and throat and voice box (larynx). Most <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> are squamous cell <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span>. They begin in the moist tissues that line the <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span>. The <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> cells may spread into deeper tissue as the <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> grows.</p><p>There are other <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> that develop in the <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span>, such as brain <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, eye <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, and esophageal <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. But they are usually not considered to be <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span>, because those types of <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> and their treatments are different.</p>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>? <p>Anyone can get <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, but you are more likely to develop it if you:</p><ul><li>Use tobacco or drink lots of alcohol. Your risk of developing <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> is even higher if you do both.</li><li>Are male.</li><li>Are over age 50.</li><li>Have a history of <span class="qt0">head</span> or <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Have HPV (for <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> in the tonsils and base of the tongue).</li><li>Are exposed to wood dusts or certain other toxic substances at work (for upper throat, nose, and sinus <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span>).</li><li>Have had radiation exposure to the <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> (for salivary gland <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>).</li><li>Have Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (for upper throat and salivary gland <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span>).</li><li>Are Asian (for upper throat <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>).</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p>The symptoms of <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span throat that does not go away</li><li>Trouble swallowing</li><li>A change or hoarseness in the voice</li></ul><p>Other possible symptoms can depend on the specific type of <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>.</p>How is <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>Which exams and tests used to diagnose <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> can depend on the specific type of <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. Possible exams and tests may include:</p><ul><li>A physical exam of the area that might have <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Blood and/or urine tests.</li><li>An endoscopy.</li><li>A biopsy or other procedure to collect cells from the area that might have <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. The cells are viewed under a microscope to find out if they are abnormal.</li><li>Imaging tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p>The treatment for <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> will depend on the specific type of <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, the stage (how advanced the <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> is), your overall health, and other factors. The treatment options might include:</p><ul><li>Surgery</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span> immunotherapy</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that mainly attack specific <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> cells and cause less harm to normal cells</li></ul><p>In some cases, you may need a combination of treatments. Sometimes surgery can affect how well you can chew, swallow, or talk. Rehabilitation, such as physical therapy, dietary counseling, and speech therapy, may help.</p>Can <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to help prevent <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol use or not drinking at all</li><li>Getting regular dental exams</li><li>Talking to your provider about HPV vaccination</li></ul><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>? <p>Oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer is cancer</span></span> of the mouth. It is a type of <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. Most oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> are squamous cell <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span>. They begin in the flat cells that cover the surfaces of your mouth, tongue, and lips. The <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> cells may spread into deeper tissue as the <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> grows.</p><p>Most oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> are related to tobacco use, heavy alcohol use, or an HPV infection.</p>Who is more likely to develop oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p>Anyone can get oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, but you are more likely to develop it if you:</p><ul><li>Use tobacco or drink lots of alcohol. Your risk of developing oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> is even higher if you do both.</li><li>Are male.</li><li>Are over ago 40.</li><li>Have HPV.</li><li>Have a history of <span class="qt0">head</span> or <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Get frequent sun exposure (for lip <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>).</li></ul>What are the symptoms of oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p>The symptoms of oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>A white or red patch in your mouth</li><li>A lip or mouth sore that won't heal</li><li>Bleeding, pain, or numbness in the lip or mouth</li><li>Loose teeth or dentures that no longer fit well</li><li>Problems or pain with swallowing</li><li>A lump in your <span class="qt1">neck</span></li><li>Ear pain</li><li>Trouble moving your mouth or jaw</li><li>Swelling of the jaw</li><li>A sore throat or feeling that something is caught in the throat</li></ul><p>If you have any of these symptoms for more than two weeks, see your health care provider or dentist. Oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> can spread quickly, so it's important to find it early.</p>How is oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, your provider may use:</p><ul><li>A physical exam of the lips and mouth.</li><li>An endoscopy.</li><li>A biopsy or other procedure to collect cells from the lip or oral cavity. The cells are viewed under a microscope to find out if they are abnormal.</li><li>Imaging tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p>The treatments for oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> include surgery, radiation therapy, or both. After surgery, some people also need chemotherapy to kill any <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> cells that are left.</p>Can oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to help prevent oral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol use or not drinking at all</li><li>Getting regular dental exams</li></ul><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Throat <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> is a type of <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. Throat <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> has different names, depending on which part of the throat is affected. The different parts of your throat are called the oropharynx, the hypopharynx, the nasopharynx, and the larynx, or voice box.</p><p>The main risk factors for throat <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> are tobacco use and heavy drinking. Certain types of throat <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> also have other risk factors. For example, having HPV is a risk factor for oropharyngeal <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>Symptoms of throat <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>A sore throat that does not go away</li><li>A lump in the <span class="qt1">neck</span></li><li>Pain or ringing in the ears</li><li>Trouble swallowing</li><li>Ear pain</li></ul><p>To diagnose throat <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span>, doctors may do a physical exam and history, imaging tests, and a biopsy. You may also need other tests, depending on the type of <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. Treatments include surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. Treatment for some types of throat <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> may also include targeted therapy. Targeted therapy uses drugs or other substances that attack specific <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> cells with less harm to normal cells.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hpv.html">
      <content name="title">HPV</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">HPV Vaccine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Human Papillomavirus</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is HPV?<p>Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a group of more than 200 related viruses. Some of them are spread through sexual contact. Most people have been exposed to HPV. Usually, your immune system controls HPV infections, and they go away on their own and don't cause any health problems, but some need treatment.</p><p>There are two categories of sexually transmitted HPV. They are called low-risk HPV and high-risk HPV. Sometimes high-risk HPV infections can stay at the cervix (the lower part of a woman's uterus) for many years. This can lead to cell changes. If these changes are not screened for and treated, they may get worse over time and become <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>Low-risk HPVM can cause warts on or around your genitals, anus, mouth, or throat.</p><p>High-risk HPV can cause various <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span>:</p><ul><li>Cervical <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span></li><li>Anal <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span></li><li>Oropharyngeal <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, a type of <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, also called throat <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span></li><li>Vulvar <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span></li><li>Vaginal <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span></li><li>Penile <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span></li></ul>Who is at risk for HPV infections?<p>HPV infections are very common. Nearly all sexually active people are infected with HPV soon after they become sexually active.</p>What are the symptoms of HPV infections?<p>Some people get warts from certain low-risk HPV infections, but the other types (including the high-risk types) have no symptoms.</p><p>If a high-risk HPV infection lasts for many years and causes cell changes, you may have symptoms. You may also have symptoms if those cell changes develop into <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. Which symptoms you have depends on which part of your body is affected.</p>How are HPV infections diagnosed?<p>Health care providers can usually find out if you have warts by looking at them.</p><p>Nearly all cervical <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> are caused by a long-lasting infection with a high-risk type of HPV. Screening can prevent <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> by finding out if you need treatment for changes that might happen before <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, called precancer.</p><p>Screening tests for HPV can include:</p><ul><li>For women, there are cervical <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> screening tests that can find changes in the cervix that might lead to <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. As part of the screening, women may have Pap tests (sometimes called a Pap smear),  HPV tests,  or both. HPV tests use a sample of cervical cells.</li><li>Your provider may also suggest a colposcopy  to check for abnormal cells.</li></ul>What are the treatments for HPV infections?<p>An HPV infection itself cannot be treated. Because HPV causes <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> at other places in the body, testing for the HPV virus can be helpful to make other treatment decisions.</p><ul><li>HPV infection. Talk to your provider about whether you need other tests and how often you should be checked to prevent cervical <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Warts. There are medicines that you can apply to a wart. If they don't work, your provider could freeze, burn, or surgically remove them.</li><li>Cell changes caused by infection with high-risk HPV. Treatments may include medicines you apply to the affected area or various surgical procedures.</li></ul><p>People who have HPV-related <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> usually get the same types of treatment as people who have <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> that HPV does not cause. An exception to this is for people who have certain oral and throat <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span>. They may have different treatment options.</p>Can HPV infections be prevented?<p>Correct usage of latex condoms greatly reduces, but does not completely eliminate, the risk of catching or spreading HPV. If you or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms. The most reliable way to avoid infection is to not have anal, vaginal, or oral sex.</p><p>Vaccines can protect against several types of HPV, including genital warts and some that can cause <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. The vaccines provide the most protection when people get them before exposure to the virus. This means that it is best for people to get them before they become sexually active.</p><p>Ask your child's provider about when to vaccinate your child against HPV. If you're over age 26 and haven't been vaccinated, talk with your provider about the possible benefits of vaccination.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your salivary glands make saliva - sometimes called spit - and empty it into your mouth through openings called ducts. Saliva makes your food moist, which helps you chew and swallow. It helps you digest your food. It also cleans your mouth and contains antibodies that can kill germs.</p><p>Salivary gland <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> is a type of <span class="qt0">head</span> and <span class="qt1">neck</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. It is rare. It may not cause any symptoms, or you could notice:</p><ul><li>A lump in your ear, cheek, jaw, lip, or inside the mouth</li><li>Fluid draining from your ear</li><li>Trouble swallowing or opening the mouth widely</li><li>Numbness, weakness, or pain in your face</li></ul><p>Doctors diagnose salivary gland <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> using a physical exam, imaging tests, and a biopsy. Treatment can include surgery, radiation therapy, and/or chemotherapy.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>
